subject: Return values derived from variables declared in the Model Block

messages.author: d57a3987c2bce75f
messages.subject: Return values derived from variables declared in the Model Block
parts:
I am working on an ARMA model similar to the one described on page 67 of the Stan manual.  I am trying to return the last calculated error ("err") to R with rstan.  However, defining "err" as a parameter rather than declaring it in the model block leads to an error:

"Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  : 
  failed to parse Stan model 'checkARMA' with error message:
SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
attempt to assign variable in wrong block. left-hand-side variable origin=parameter"

The last error value in an ARMA model is useful for projecting the data forward.

Attached is a test model.  Essentially, I am just looking to return the last calculated value of "err" to R.  I am not sure how to get the value either through the "generated quantities" or "transformed parameter" block.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Return values derived from variables declared in the Model Block
parts:
Here's the model in question:

model {
real err;
mu ~ normal(0,10);
phi ~ normal(0,2);
theta ~ normal(0,2);
sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
err <- y[1] - mu + phi * mu;
err ~ normal(0,sigma);
for (t in 2:T) {
err <- y[t] - (mu + phi * y[t-1] + theta * err);
err ~ normal(0,sigma);
}
}

There's not a good way to save just the last err value
here from the model as written. Some alternatives:

1. Define err[T] as an array in transformed parameters and use
that. It will save too much output, but at least you'll get the last
value and you get the added benefit of vectorizing the normal, which
is a substantial speedup.

transformed parameters {
real err[T]; // this saves all the err values
err[1] <- y[1] - mu + phi * mu;
for (t in 2:T)
err[t] <- y[t] - (mu + phi * y[t-1] + theta * err[t-1]);
}
model {
...
err ~ normal(0,sigma); // now it's vectorized
}


2. Recompute err in generated quantities and save the last one.

generated quantities {
real last_err:
last_err <- y[1] - mu + phi * mu;
for (t in 2:T)
last_err <- y[t] - (mu + phi * y[t-1] + theta * last_err);
}

and you'll get just what you need. The computation's basically
free inside of generated quantities because it involves double
values rather than autodiff vars.

3. Write a function to define the err vector and use it in
both places.

functions {
real[] errs(real[] y, real mu, real phi, real theta) {
real[size(y)] result;
result[1] <- y[1] - mu + phi * mu;
for (t in 2:size(y))
result[t] <- y[t] - (mu + phi * y[t-1] + theta * result[t-1]);
return result;
}

Then your model can be:

errs(y,mu,phi,theta) ~ normal(0,sigma);

And then in generated quantities you can just set a value to

last_err <- errs(y,mu,phi,theta)[T].

This is best for speed and minimum output.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Return values derived from variables declared in the Model Block
parts:
For observed data, you can do an AR(1) model like

model {
  real y_lag[T];
  /* do something about T[1] like modeling it or conditioning on it */
  for(t in 2:T) y_lag[t] <- y[t-1];
  y ~ normal(mu + phi * y_lag, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  real err;
  {
    real y_lag;
    y_lag <- 0;
    for(t in 1:(T-1))
      y_lag <- mu + phi * y_lag + normal_rng(0,sigma);
  }
  err <- y[T] - y_lag;
}

That is not quite what you asked for, but it might be want.

Ben

parts:
Thank you for the speedy response!  Ben's answer appears similar to Bob's except for the addition of the "+ normal_rng(0,sigma)" to the estimated y value.


With regard to Andrew's question, I think the likelihood of y[1]  is not included.  According to the Stan manual (pg 59) "The first observed data point, y[1], is not modeled here because there is nothing to
condition on; instead, it acts to condition y[2]".

Bob - thanks for the option 3 version.  It looks like option 2 is the easiest to implement.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Return values derived from variables declared in the Model Block
parts:
You can model it if you want. You just need a different
model because you don't have anything to condition on. Which
then gives you nothing to estimate a scale based on, so you'll
need a fixed scale or some input of where to start.

The + normal_rng(0,sigma) will add normal(0,sigma) noise.

- Bob
